title: Methylene Blue -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Methylene blue is a multifaceted therapeutic agent used across a wide range of clinical settings, with its well-established role being the Food and Drug Administration–approved treatment for acquired methemoglobinemia. The unique redox properties of methylene blue enable the restoration of functional hemoglobin and enhanced oxygen delivery, making it a critical intervention in toxicologic emergencies. Beyond this indication, methylene blue has demonstrated clinical utility in perioperative care, critical illness, and select neurologic and oncologic procedures, underscoring the importance of a thorough understanding of its mechanisms, benefits, and potential risks for clinicians across specialties.

title: Methylene Blue -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity provides a comprehensive review of methylene blue, including Food and Drug Administration–approved and commonly recognized off-label uses such as vasoplegic shock, ifosfamide-induced encephalopathy, and intraoperative staining, as well as emerging applications in neuroprotective and psychiatric research. Learners will explore evidence-based dosing and administration strategies, key contraindications, and clinically significant adverse effects, including hemolysis, serotonin syndrome, anaphylaxis, and interference with diagnostic monitoring. Emphasis is placed on patient selection, safety monitoring, and interprofessional collaboration to support informed decision-making and optimize patient outcomes in diverse clinical environments.

title: Methylene Blue -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify approved and commonly used off-label indications for methylene blue. Implement evidence-based monitoring strategies in patients receiving methylene blue to detect adverse effects such as hemolysis, serotonin syndrome, anaphylaxis, and neurologic toxicity. title: Methylene Blue -- Indications
content: Methylene blue is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a treatment for acquired methemoglobinemia, a condition in which hemoglobin iron is oxidized from the ferrous (Fe 2+ ) to ferric (Fe 3+ ) state. Ferric iron is unable to bind oxygen effectively, resulting in impaired oxygen delivery, reduced oxygen saturation, and subsequent tissue hypoxia.

title: Methylene Blue -- Mechanism of Action
content: Methylene blue exerts its pharmacological effect primarily as a redox agent and alternative electron carrier. In the treatment of methemoglobinemia, methylene blue is reduced by NADPH-dependent methemoglobin reductase to leucomethylene blue, which then reduces Fe 3+ in methemoglobin back to the ferrous state Fe 2+ , restoring normal hemoglobin function. This nonenzymatic redox conversion is the primary mechanism by which methylene blue reverses methemoglobinemia.

title: Methylene Blue -- Mechanism of Action
content: Vitamin C exhibits similar reducing properties and can serve as an alternative treatment for methemoglobinemia, though with significant limitations. Ascorbic acid reduces methemoglobin through a slower, nonenzymatic pathway that often requires multiple doses over several hours to achieve a significant effect. [3] [5] Although case reports demonstrate successful treatment with high-dose vitamin C, it is unlikely to be effective in a resuscitation situation. Vitamin C is most appropriate when methylene blue is contraindicated—such as in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency—or when methylene blue is unavailable. [3] [5] [11]

title: Methylene Blue -- Mechanism of Action
content: At the cellular level, methylene blue can bypass dysfunctional components of the mitochondrial electron transport chain by shuttling electrons from NADH, in the presence of complex I, and donating them directly to cytochrome c, effectively bypassing complexes I through III. [9] [10] This alternative electron transfer pathway enhances mitochondrial respiration, increases oxygen consumption, reduces mitochondrial superoxide production, and mitigates oxidative stress—mechanisms that underlie its neuroprotective effects in conditions such as Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, traumatic brain injury, and stroke. [9] [12] Additionally, methylene blue inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase, contributing to its vasoconstrictive effects in the management of vasoplegic shock. [7]

title: Methylene Blue -- Mechanism of Action
content: Methylene blue inhibits both nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase, contributing to its vasoconstrictive effects in vasoplegic shock. [13] [14] By inhibiting the nitric oxide-guanylate cyclase-cyclic guanosine monophosphate pathway, methylene blue attenuates the excessive vasodilation mediated by inflammatory cytokines in septic and post-cardiopulmonary bypass vasoplegic shock. [13] [14]

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: The dosing and administration of methylene blue vary depending on the indication, patient characteristics, and clinical setting. Although standardized regimens exist for the treatment of acquired methemoglobinemia, many other uses are off-label and supported primarily by clinical experience, case series, and institutional protocols. Careful attention to dosing, infusion timing, and patient-specific factors is essential to optimize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing adverse effects.

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: In both pediatric and adult patients, methylene blue is administered intravenously at a dose of 1 mg/kg over 5 to 30 minutes. A repeat dose of 1 mg/kg may be given after 1 hour if methemoglobin levels remain above 30% or symptoms persist. If the condition does not resolve after 2 doses, alternative treatment strategies should be considered.

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: In patients with moderate-to-severe renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate 15-59 mL/min/1.73 m²), the recommended regimen is a single intravenous dose of 1 mg/kg. If methemoglobin levels remain elevated or symptoms persist after 1 hour, alternative therapies should be pursued.

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: For intraoperative lymph node mapping, 1 to 5 mL of 1% methylene blue is injected peritumorally, subareolarly, or pericervically, depending on the tumor type and anatomical site. The dye migrates through lymphatic channels, allowing visual identification of sentinel lymph nodes to guide surgical staging and resection.

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: Methylene blue has been evaluated at a dose of 50 mg (2 mL of a 2.5% solution) administered intravenously approximately 45 seconds before propofol injection. Although this approach has demonstrated efficacy in reducing injection-related pain, it is not standard practice, and lidocaine remains the preferred agent. [15]

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: For the treatment of ifosfamide-induced neurotoxicity, methylene blue is typically administered intravenously at a dosage of 50 mg every 4 hours until symptom resolution. This regimen is supported by case series and institutional experience; however, dosing is individualized based on clinical response, with symptom resolution often occurring within 10 minutes to 24 hours. [16] [17] [18]

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: In vasoplegic shock, methylene blue is commonly administered as a single intravenous bolus of 2 mg/kg over 20 to 30 minutes. Some protocols incorporate a bolus followed by continuous infusion; however, evidence supporting routine preoperative or postoperative prophylactic use to reduce mortality remains limited, and this practice is not considered standard of care. [19] [20] [21]

title: Methylene Blue -- Administration
content: Methylene blue, used for parathyroid gland identification during parathyroidectomy, may be administered at a dose of 0.4 mg/kg intravenously 1 hour before surgery. However, this practice has fallen out of favor at many institutions due to concerns about neurotoxicity, particularly at higher cumulative doses (>5 mg/kg). Lower doses are increasingly preferred. [22] [23]

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects
content: Methylene blue is generally well-tolerated but carries several critical adverse effects and contraindications that clinicians must consider when treating methemoglobinemia or using it for off-label indications. The most commonly reported adverse reactions include headache, hypokalemia, diarrhea, hypomagnesemia, myoclonus, nausea, and seizure-like phenomena. Additional adverse effects include hemolytic anemia; cardiovascular effects, such as palpitations, tachycardia, and hypertension; gastrointestinal disturbances; and blue-green discoloration of urine, which is expected and benign.

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Serotonin Syndrome
content: Serotonin syndrome has been reported following administration of methylene blue, particularly when used concomitantly with medications that increase serotonergic activity, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and monoamine oxidase inhibitors; certain opioids; and dextromethorphan. The risk is increased with concurrent use, and fatal cases have been described. Clinical manifestations include the following: Altered mental status: Agitation, hallucinations, delirium, or coma); Autonomic instability: Tachycardia, labile blood pressure, dizziness, diaphoresis, flushing, and hyperthermia Neuromuscular abnormalities: Tremor, rigidity, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, and incoordination Seizures Gastrointestinal symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Serotonin Syndrome
content: Concomitant use of methylene blue with serotonergic agents and opioids should be avoided. Patients receiving methylene blue should be closely monitored for signs and symptoms of serotonin syndrome; if suspected, methylene blue should be discontinued and supportive care initiated promptly. Patients should be counseled regarding this risk and advised to avoid serotonergic medications for at least 72 hours following the final dose of methylene blue.

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Anaphylaxis
content: Anaphylactic reactions have been reported in patients receiving methylene blue. Patients should be closely monitored for signs of hypersensitivity, including angioedema, urticaria, and bronchospasm. If anaphylaxis or other severe hypersensitivity reactions occur, methylene blue should be discontinued immediately and appropriate supportive care initiated.

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Hemolytic Anemia
content: Hemolysis may occur during the treatment of methemoglobinemia with methylene blue. Laboratory findings can include Heinz bodies, elevated indirect bilirubin, decreased haptoglobin, and a negative direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test. Anemia may develop 1 or more days after administration and, in severe cases, may require red blood cell transfusion. To minimize risk, the lowest effective number of methylene blue doses should be used, and the drug should be discontinued if significant hemolysis develops. Alternative therapies for methemoglobinemia should be considered.

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Hemolytic Anemia
content: Hemolysis associated with methylene blue therapy is mechanistically linked to its oxidative properties, which can overwhelm erythrocyte antioxidant defenses, particularly in susceptible individuals. The American Heart Association emphasizes that patients with G6PD deficiency are at markedly increased risk, as impaired NADPH generation limits glutathione regeneration, rendering red blood cells unable to counteract oxidative stress and predisposing to rapid hemolysis and worsening anemia. [3] [5]

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Encephalopathy
content: In clinical trials, methylene blue treatment has been associated with central nervous system adverse effects, including confusion, dizziness, and visual disturbances. Patients should be advised to avoid driving, operating heavy or potentially hazardous machinery, or engaging in activities requiring full alertness until these symptoms have fully resolved, as such effects may impair safe task performance.

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Interference with Clinical Monitoring and Laboratory Assays
content: The presence of methylene blue in the bloodstream can cause pulse oximetry to significantly underestimate true oxygen saturation by interfering with the device's measurement wavelengths. During and shortly after methylene blue infusion, arterial blood gas analysis with direct measurement of oxygen saturation (SaO 2 ) should be used instead of pulse oximetry to accurately assess oxygenation.

title: Methylene Blue -- Adverse Effects -- Interference with Clinical Monitoring and Laboratory Assays
content: Methylene blue is excreted in the urine and, because of its blue coloration, may interfere with urinatlysis methods that rely on colorimetric indicators, such as dipstick testing for leukocyte esterase, potentially resulting in false-negative or uninterpretable results. When accurate urine testing is clinically necessary, alternative diagnostic approaches or repeat testing after dye clearance should be considered.

title: Methylene Blue -- Contraindications
content: Due to the risk of hemolysis and worsening anemia, methylene blue is contraindicated in patients with G6PD deficiency. [3] In addition, it is contraindicated in individuals with a known history of anaphylaxis or other severe hypersensitivity reactions to methylene blue or related thiazine dye products, given reports of life-threatening allergic reactions.

title: Methylene Blue -- Contraindications
content: Although not an absolute contraindication, methylene blue may cause fetal harm when administered during pregnancy. Intra-amniotic administration of methylene blue–containing products, particularly during the second trimester, has been associated with serious fetal adverse outcomes, including intestinal atresia and fetal demise. When methylene blue is administered hours to days before delivery, reported neonatal complications include hyperbilirubinemia, hemolytic anemia, blue skin discoloration, methemoglobinemia, respiratory distress, and photosensitivity.

title: Methylene Blue -- Contraindications
content: Newborns exposed to methylene blue in utero, especially near term, should be closely monitored for these adverse effects. Management is primarily supportive and may include phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia, red blood cell transfusion for hemolytic anemia, supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support for respiratory distress, and protection from light to reduce photosensitivity. Serial laboratory monitoring of bilirubin, hemoglobin, and methemoglobin levels is recommended to guide clinical management.

title: Methylene Blue -- Monitoring
content: Methylene blue is generally well tolerated at therapeutic doses below 2 mg/kg; however, doses exceeding 7 mg/kg are associated with a markedly increased risk of adverse effects. [24] The FDA labeling carries a boxed warning stating that methylene blue may cause serious or fatal serotonin syndrome when used in combination with serotonergic drugs—including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and monoamine oxidase inhibitors—and opioids, and recommends avoiding concomitant use entirely. [25] Caution is also warranted in patients with renal impairment, as methylene blue may reduce renal blood flow. [24] .

title: Methylene Blue -- Toxicity
content: Methylene blue demonstrates clear dose-dependent toxicity thresholds. At single doses of 3 mg/kg or more, hypotension, wheezing, and reduced oxygenation have been reported. Cumulative doses of 7 mg/kg or more can cause significant toxicity, including nausea, vomiting, precordial pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, chest tightness, tachycardia, apprehension, tremor, mydriasis, abdominal pain, dizziness, paresthesia, headache, confusion, and mild methemoglobinemia (up to 7%), with effects lasting 2 to 12 hours. [24] Severe overdosage (single dose of 20 mg/kg or more) has caused severe intravascular hemolysis, hyperbilirubinemia, and death.
